Swine
swīne
n. (the pig; the standing biblical emblem of the unclean; rendering Hebrew chazir, Greek choiros)
From Anglo-Saxon swin. In Scripture the swine is not merely unclean but the type of uncleanness, the animal by which apostasy is measured.

Biblical Definition

Swine is declared unclean by a precise test: “the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you” (Lev 11:7). The detail matters. The pig has the outward mark and lacks the inward process — the right feet, the wrong digestion — which makes it a natural emblem of the hypocrite. Deuteronomy adds that Israel must not even touch the carcase (Deu 14:8). By Isaiah's day, eating swine's flesh among the graves is the shorthand for a people gone entirely over to abomination (Isa 65:4), and Isaiah 66:3 sets swine's blood beside legitimate sacrifice to show that worship offered wrongly is not partial obedience but its opposite. Proverbs makes the sharpest single use: “As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion” (Pro 11:22). And the Lord Jesus forbids the casting of pearls before them (Mat 7:6) — a warning about wasting holy things on those who will only trample and turn.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines swine as a hog, a pachydermatous quadruped — noting that the word is used both as singular and plural, and that swine were unclean by the Mosaic law.

SWINE, n. sing. and plu. A hog; a pachydermatous quadruped of the genus Sus.

The swine, though he divide the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you. Lev. xi.

Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine. Matt. vii.

Swine's flesh was forbidden to the Israelites as an abomination.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:7 — "And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you."

Pro 11:22 — "As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion."

Mat 7:6 — "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you."

Isa 65:4 — "Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;"

Modern Corruption

Discernment itself treated as the sin — any refusal to give holy things to those who trample them called judgmental — where Christ commands exactly that refusal.

expand to see more

Matthew 7:6 stands immediately after judge not, and the placement is deliberate: the same paragraph that forbids hypocritical condemnation commands a discriminating judgment about who receives what. Casting pearls before swine is forbidden, and obeying that requires deciding, about actual people, that they will trample and rend. A church that has been shamed out of all discernment cannot obey verse 6, and generally supposes it is being especially faithful to verse 1.

Leviticus 11:7 supplies the reason the pig became the emblem it is. The animal has the correct external mark — the divided hoof, visible to anyone — and lacks the internal one, the chewing of the cud, which no observer sees. That is the anatomy of hypocrisy exactly, and it is why Proverbs 11:22 lands so hard: a gold ring in a pig's snout is ornament attached to something that will take it straight back into the mud. Outward adornment cannot compensate for the missing inward work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazir (H2386), swine, boar — the boar out of the wood that wastes the vine (Psa 80:13); Greek choiros (G5519), a young pig — the Gadarene herd and the prodigal's husks.

expand to see more

Hebrew chazir (H2386) — swine; unclean by the test of Lev 11:7, and the emblem of apostate feasting in Isa 65:4.

Greek choiros (G5519) — a swine; the herd into which the legion was sent (Mat 8:30), and the swine the prodigal was sent to feed (Luk 15:15).

Greek hus (G5300) — a sow; the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire (2Pe 2:22), nature unchanged by washing.

Usage

"“He cheweth not the cud; he is unclean” — the right feet, the wrong digestion."

"“As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout” — ornament on something that returns to the mud."

"“Neither cast ye your pearls before swine” — a command requiring discernment."
